dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?
Hi, Anita. Thomas Wilcox here. I'm looking to put up a fence and I wanted to find out what the rules are.
Sure, I can help with that. Is this for a property in Newport?
Yeah, it's a rental I own. I'm the landlord. I'd rather not get into the exact address right now, I just want the general picture.
That's fine. Tell me what you have in mind. Where would the fence go, and how tall?
Along the back property line. I was thinking six feet. Well, the boards would be five feet tall, pressure-treated wood. So I'm saying six because of the posts and a little gap at the bottom.
Okay, so let me make sure I have it. The fence itself is about five feet, but with the posts and the gap the overall height could come to six feet?
Right, the whole thing standing could be six. The boards are five.

Got it. That's the number that matters, the overall height. So to your main question, yes, a fence generally does need a permit here, and the height is one of the things that gets looked at. Six feet in the back is on the taller side, so I'd plan on filing paperwork.
So I do need a permit. I wasn't sure, because my brother-in-law put one up years ago and he said nobody bothered him.

A lot of people say that, but I wouldn't count on it. If a neighbor complains or the property gets inspected, you could be asked to take it down or apply after the fact. It's easier to do it up front.
Fair enough. What does the paperwork look like? What do you need from me?
Generally an application, a sketch or survey showing where the fence goes in relation to the property lines, the height, and the materials. Do you have a survey of the lot?
I think so. There's one in the file from when I bought it. It's old, though. Does it matter?
An older survey is usually fine as a starting point, as long as the lot hasn't changed. Are there any other structures near that back line? A shed, a garage, anything like that?

There's a little shed over on the left side, but it's a few feet off the line. Nothing else back there. Past the line it's the neighbor's yard, and then you hit the lane that runs behind, where the old gas station was.
Okay. I'd mark the shed on your sketch too. And is the property in a historic district, do you know?
Hm. I don't think so. How would I find out?
When you give us the address, we can tell you. It can change the rules on materials and height, so it's worth checking before you buy lumber.
Okay, I'll hold off on the lumber. Next question. How long does approval take? I'd like to get it done in the spring.

For a simple fence it's usually fairly quick, often a matter of days to a couple of weeks once the application is complete. If it needs extra review, like a historic district, it can take longer. Spring should be realistic if you apply soon.
That's better than I figured. Can I turn it in by email, or do I have to come down?
You can come to the office at City Hall, and the forms are on the city website too. If you tell me the address, I can also have someone confirm whether anything special applies.

I'll look it up and call back with that. [pause] Can I say something? I inspect elevators for a living, so I spend my days dealing with codes and people who argue about them. This call is a relief. You just answered the question.
Well, I'm glad it's been easy. Elevators, that's a serious job. Nobody thinks about it until it stops.
That's about right. Alright, so permit, survey, sketch with the shed on it, check on the historic thing. Did I miss anything?
That covers it. Also keep the overall height in mind when you fill out the form, six feet with the posts. And if you want to ask anything else, call us back and ask for zoning.
Will do. Thanks, Anita. Happy New Year.
You too, Mr. Wilcox. Happy New Year. Take care.
